Quantum algorithm for one-quasiparticle excitations in the thermodynamic limit via cluster-additive block diagonalization

Preprint: APS/123-QED
Sumeet Email: sumeet.sumeet@fau.de Affiliation: Department of Physics, Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU), 91058 Erlangen, Germany    M. Hörmann Affiliation: Department of Physics, Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU), 91058 Erlangen, Germany    K. P. Schmidt Affiliation: Department of Physics, Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU), 91058 Erlangen, Germany
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We propose a quantum algorithm for computing one-quasiparticle excitation energies in the thermodynamic limit by combining numerical linked-cluster expansions (NLCEs) and the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE). Our approach uses VQE to block-diagonalize the cluster Hamiltonian through a single-unitary transformation. This unitary is then postprocessed using the projective cluster-additive transformation (PCAT) to ensure cluster additivity, a key requirement for NLCE convergence. We benchmark our method on the transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) in one and two dimensions, and with longitudinal field, computing one-quasiparticle dispersions in the high-field polarized phase. We compare two cost function classes, trace minimization and variance based, demonstrating their effectiveness with the Hamiltonian variational ansatz (HVA). For pure TFIM, ⌈N/2⌉\lceil N/2\rceil layers of HVA suffice: NLCE+VQE matches exact diagonalization. For TFIM with longitudinal field, where parity symmetry breaks and PCAT becomes essential, both ⌈N/2⌉\lceil N/2\rceil and NN layers of HVA converge with increasing cluster size, with NN layers providing improved accuracy. Our results establish PCAT as a cluster-additive framework that extends variational quantum algorithms to excited-state calculations in the thermodynamic limit via NLCE. While demonstrated with VQE, the PCAT postprocessing approach, which requires only low-energy eigenspace information, applies to any quantum eigenstate preparation method.

I Introduction

Understanding elementary excitations is central to the study of quantum many-body systems. Such excitations govern low-temperature thermodynamics and long-range dynamical behavior, and are directly accessible via spectroscopic techniques such as inelastic neutron or light scattering. Consequently, developing accurate and efficient methods to compute the excitation spectrum is a major objective in condensed matter physics, as well as in quantum chemistry and quantum simulation.

Recent years have witnessed significant progress in hybrid quantum-classical algorithms, particularly in using the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) [1] to compute ground-state properties of strongly correlated systems. These algorithms are particularly relevant for noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices [2], where limited qubit coherence times and gate fidelities preclude error-corrected quantum computation. Originally designed for quantum chemistry applications [1, 3], VQE has been increasingly applied to condensed matter models, including studies of quantum magnets [4, 5], spin liquids [6], frustrated systems [7, 8], quantum critical points [9, 10], and our recent numerical linked-cluster expansion (NLCE)+VQE approach for ground-state energies [11]. Recent no-go theorems have highlighted trainability challenges for variational quantum algorithms under certain assumptions [12, 13]. However, systematic exploration with problem-adapted ansätze remains essential for developing successful strategies, and our work contributes to this by exploring VQE for degenerate subspaces within the NLCE framework using physically motivated initialization.

VQE has proven successful for ground-state calculations, providing a robust method to minimize the energy expectation value on finite quantum systems. Extending these approaches to compute excited states is an important next step, with multiple strategies having been proposed. These include variational quantum deflation [14], quantum equation of motion [15], subspace-search VQE (SSVQE) [16], and other ensemble and penalty-based methods [17, 18]. Some of these techniques (such as SSVQE) can handle degenerate subspaces, though they are primarily designed for extracting individual eigenstates rather than constructing effective models for low-energy physics.

In many quantum lattice models, elementary excitations can be interpreted as quasiparticles: stable or long-lived excitations carrying a well-defined momentum k→\vec{k} and energy ω⁡(k→)\omega(\vec{k}). Constructing an effective quasiparticle Hamiltonian provides a compact description of these excitations through a few local coupling constants, reveals the underlying interaction structure, and connects directly to experimental observables.

Classical approaches to construct such effective Hamiltonians rely on block-diagonalization methods in quantum many-body physics, such as the Schrieffer-Wolff transformation [19], continuous unitary transformations  [20, 21, 22], and the contractor renormalization group [23], which aim to isolate quasiparticle sectors by transforming the full Hamiltonian into a block-diagonal form where each block conserves the number of quasiparticles. Perturbative linked-cluster expansions [24, 25] provide a systematic way to reach the thermodynamic limit by combining such block-diagonalization transformations with cluster expansion techniques. Perturbative approaches are limited to perturbative regimes. However, all of the previously mentioned methods can also be formulated non-perturbatively. Then, NLCEs [26, 27, 28, 29], meaning replacing the perturbative with the exact result on a cluster, can be used to overcome the perturbative limitation. However, the exponential scaling still limits accessible cluster sizes.

While NLCE combined with exact diagonalization (ED) has been successful for both ground states and excitations, our recent work has demonstrated NLCE+VQE for ground-state energies [11], a method where VQE is used as a cluster solver instead of ED for each finite cluster in NLCE. However, a quantum or hybrid quantum-classical analog of these NLCE methods for constructing cluster-additive effective Hamiltonians of excited states does not exist yet. Recently, VQE-based approaches have been applied to extract quasiparticle excitations from finite periodic systems [30], but these methods target individual eigenstates on finite periodic clusters rather than constructing cluster-additive transformations suitable for thermodynamic-limit extrapolation via NLCE. Extending the NLCE framework to excitations with VQE as a cluster solver presents unique challenges due to higher dimensionality of excitation subspaces on finite clusters, which requires ensuring cluster additivity, a property not automatically satisfied by standard VQE block-diagonalization unitaries.

In this work, we propose a hybrid quantum-classical method to construct an effective one-quasiparticle (1QP) Hamiltonian in the thermodynamic limit. Our approach combines VQE with NLCEs and generalizes the NLCE+VQE method that we have recently introduced for ground-state energies [11]. Extending this framework to excitations presents significant challenges: Unlike the ground-state energy (a scalar quantity), 1QP excitations form a multi-dimensional subspace on finite clusters, requiring careful treatment to maintain the cluster additivity essential for NLCE convergence.

To ensure the transformation satisfies cluster additivity, which is essential for NLCE convergence, we proceed in two stages. Within each cluster of the NLCE, we employ a VQE-based cost function to approximate a unitary transformation that decouples the ground and 1QP subspaces. From this, we construct the projective cluster-additive transformation (PCAT) [31], which guarantees cluster additivity, a property that the transformation factorizes for disconnected clusters [32]. We use a single unitary to decouple the full low-energy subspace (ground state and 1QP states) from higher excitations, rather than targeting individual eigenstates. As a result, a single VQE optimization simultaneously yields the entire NN-dimensional 1QP block on a finite cluster, from which the full dispersion ω⁡(k→)\omega(\vec{k}) in the thermodynamic limit is recovered after NLCE embedding, in contrast to approaches that obtain quasiparticle energies one momentum at a time. This block-diagonalization approach exploits the fact that energy gaps within the low-energy subspace are typically small, while gaps to higher excitations are large, facilitating efficient decoupling. We use the Hamiltonian variational ansatz (HVA) [33], which constructs the quantum circuit from the problem Hamiltonian structure, and find that a circuit depth proportional to the system size is sufficient to achieve accurate results.

As a benchmark, we apply our method to the transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) on both the one-dimensional (1D) chain and the two-dimensional (2D) square lattice, computing the 1QP dispersion in the high-field polarized phase. We demonstrate convergence of the NLCE with increasing cluster size and validate our results by comparing VQE and ED as cluster solvers. Additionally, we investigate the effect of a longitudinal field (LF) on TFIM, which breaks the parity symmetry. In this case, the ground state and 1QP excitations are no longer in different symmetry sectors, making it a particularly stringent test of our approach. The longitudinal field case requires the full machinery of PCAT to ensure cluster additivity.

Our numerical benchmarks reveal that ⌈N/2⌉\lceil N/2\rceil layers of HVA suffice for the pure TFIM, where NLCE+VQE results are indistinguishable from NLCE+ED. For TFIM+LF, convergence is slower but still achieved. We investigate two classes of cost functions (trace based and variance based) and find that both can achieve convergence, though with different initialization requirements and trade-offs discussed in Sec. V.2.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Sec. II, we provide an overview of the NLCE+VQE approach for 1QP excitations and outline the six-step workflow. Section III discusses the linked-cluster expansion for obtaining effective 1QP Hamiltonians, including details on block diagonalization (Sec. III.1), the NLCE method (Sec. III.2), the details of PCAT (Sec. III.3), and the calculation of 1QP dispersions in the thermodynamic limit (Sec. III.4). Section IV introduces VQE as the cluster solver, with details on cost functions (Sec. IV.1) and state preparation (Sec. IV.2). Section V presents numerical results for the 1QP dispersion of the high-field phase of the TFIM, including applications to the one-dimensional chain (Sec. V.1.1), the two-dimensional square lattice (Sec. V.1.2), and the TFIM+LF (Sec. V.2). We conclude in Sec. VI with a summary and outlook.

II Overview of NLCE+VQE approach for 1QP excitations

In this section, we provide an overview of our NLCE+VQE framework for computing 1QP excitations in the thermodynamic limit, outlining the key components and workflow before presenting the detailed methodology in Secs. III and IV. Here, a cluster CC is defined as a finite subset of a lattice consisting of a set of sites connected with bonds. Perturbative linked-cluster expansions (LCEs) are a common tool for calculating high-order series of excitation energies and spectral signatures of elementary excitations in the thermodynamic limit, but are limited by their perturbative nature. Practically, one performs perturbation theory on each cluster and then embeds the result in the thermodynamic limit by a proper embedding procedure. NLCEs replace the perturbation theory on finite clusters by numerical cluster solvers, typically ED for both scalar quantities and subspace calculations.

In our recent work [11], we introduced the NLCE+VQE approach for ground-state energies, which uses the VQE as a cluster solver to develop NLCEs for much larger cluster sizes in the future. Here, we extend this to 1QP excitations using VQE and PCAT to block diagonalize cluster Hamiltonians by decoupling the ground-state and 1QP subspace with a unitary UPCATU_{\mathrm{PCAT}}. Computing 1QP excitations within NLCE is substantially harder than the ground-state case. While the ground-state energy is a single scalar per cluster, the 1QP effective Hamiltonian is an N×NN\times N matrix, where NN is the number of sites in the cluster, so 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}) matrix elements must be computed instead of a single number. Moreover, NLCE embedding of non-scalar quantities is non-trivial since cluster additivity, which holds automatically for the ground-state energy, is not guaranteed for the 1QP block and must be enforced through PCAT. The transformed Hamiltonian is UPCAT†​H​UPCAT=HeffU_{\mathrm{PCAT}}^{\dagger}HU_{\mathrm{PCAT}}=H_{\mathrm{eff}}, the effective Hamiltonian. To obtain 1QP excitation energies, we extract the 1QP block of HeffH_{\mathrm{eff}} and subtract the ground-state energy.

We benchmark our approach on the TFIM, a paradigmatic quantum spin system that exhibits a quantum phase transition. The Hamiltonian for the TFIM with an optional longitudinal field is given by

H=−h∑νZν−J∑⟨ν′,ν⟩Xν′Xν−hl∑νXν,H=-h\sum_{\nu}Z_{\nu}-J\sum_{\langle\nu^{\prime},\nu\rangle}X_{\nu^{\prime}}X_{\nu^{\phantom{\prime}}}-h_{l}\sum_{\nu}X_{\nu}, (1)

where ZνZ_{\nu} and XνX_{\nu} denote Pauli matrices at site ν\nu, JJ is the nearest-neighbor Ising coupling, hh is the transverse-field strength, and hlh_{l} is the longitudinal field. We set h=1h=1 as our energy unit throughout this work. We investigate three cases: (1) the one-dimensional TFIM chain (hl=0h_{l}=0, Sec. V.1.1), (2) the two-dimensional TFIM on the square lattice (hl=0h_{l}=0, Sec. V.1.2), and (3) the one-dimensional TFIM with longitudinal field (hl≠0h_{l}\neq 0, Sec. V.2). The longitudinal field breaks the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} parity symmetry, making the third case a particularly stringent test where PCAT becomes essential for ensuring cluster additivity. The expansion is developed in the high-field polarized phase (J<hJ<h), where the ground state is gapped and 1QP excitations correspond to localized spin flips.

We explain the workflow of our NLCE+VQE approach for 1QP energies in a stepwise fashion (see Fig. 1).

  • •

    Step 1: Define the model. Choose a gapped quantum lattice model such as the TFIM+LF in Eq. (1).

  • •

    Step 2: Decompose the lattice for NLCE. Generate topologically distinct, connected finite clusters CC. We use rectangular graph expansions for lattice decomposition, which takes the clusters of dimensions Lm×Ln≤NmaxL_{m}\times L_{n}\leq N_{\mathrm{max}}, as detailed in Sec. III.2.

  • •

    Step 3: Solve each cluster using VQE. Block diagonalize each cluster CC by minimizing a cost function (Sec. IV.1) to find optimal variational parameters θ\theta such that Hdec,C=UVQE,C†​(θ)​HC​UVQE,C​(θ)H_{\mathrm{dec},C}=U^{\dagger}_{\mathrm{VQE},C}(\theta)H_{C}U_{\mathrm{VQE},C}(\theta) decouples the ground-state and 1QP subspace from the rest of the spectrum.

  • •

    Step 4: Construct cluster-additive unitary using PCAT. Use the PCAT scheme (Sec. III.3) to construct a unitary UPCAT,CU_{\mathrm{PCAT},C} from UVQE,CU_{\mathrm{VQE},C}, yielding the effective Hamiltonian Heff,C=UPCAT,C†​HC​UPCAT,CH_{\mathrm{eff},C}=U^{\dagger}_{\mathrm{PCAT},C}H_{C}U^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{\mathrm{PCAT},C}. This transformation ensures cluster additivity: Reduced contributions of disconnected clusters vanish.

  • •

    Step 5: Perform NLCE embeddings. Extract the 1QP effective Hamiltonian Heff,C[1]H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},C} from Heff,CH_{\mathrm{eff},C} and subtract the ground-state energy EC[0]E^{[0]}_{C}, which is obtained from the same VQE procedure (see Sec. IV.1). Compute the reduced contributions H¯eff,C[1]\bar{H}^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},C} using the inclusion-exclusion principle [Eq. 7] and embed into the infinite lattice, yielding Heff[1]H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff}} in the thermodynamic limit.

  • •

    Step 6: Compute the 1QP dispersion.
    Diagonalize the effective 1QP Hamiltonian (obtained in Step 5) through Fourier transform, as described in Sec. III.4, to obtain the 1QP dispersion ω⁡(k→)\omega(\vec{k}).

Finally, let us stress that PCAT is indeed a necessary ingredient of our approach. NLCEs require observables to be cluster additive, restricting calculations to connected finite clusters with disconnected parts contributing zero. For degenerate subspaces without symmetries, infinitely many unitaries can decouple the Hamiltonian, but most violate cluster additivity. The unitary UVQEU_{\mathrm{VQE}} from VQE does not satisfy cluster additivity. Furthermore, unitaries must show consistency across clusters for NLCE convergence. VQE efficiently extracts the information needed for PCAT: energy expectation values and overlaps with unperturbed eigenstates from the low-energy subspace. Crucially, PCAT requires only this low-energy eigenspace information, without needing access to higher excitation sectors, avoiding exponentially costly state tomography. This suffices to construct the PCAT [31], UPCATU_{\mathrm{PCAT}}, from UVQEU_{\mathrm{VQE}}, ensuring cluster additivity. Embedding the 1QP block of HeffH_{\mathrm{eff}} into the infinite lattice via NLCE yields the effective 1QP Hamiltonian and dispersion ω⁡(k→)\omega(\vec{k}) in the thermodynamic limit.

The computational cost is highly nonuniform across the six steps. Steps 1, 2, 5, and 6 are classical and scale polynomially with the number of clusters, while Steps 3 and 4 carry the quantum cost. The VQE optimization in Step 3 is the dominant bottleneck. Step 4 requires a single round of 𝒪⁡(N2)\mathcal{O}(N^{2}) measurements on the converged circuit to extract the matrices needed for PCAT, and avoids the exponential cost of full state tomography.

III Linked-cluster expansion for effective one-quasiparticle picture

In this section, we establish the mathematical and computational framework for extracting 1QP excitations in the thermodynamic limit using NLCEs. We first introduce the concept of block diagonalization and explain why cluster additivity is essential for NLCE convergence. We then present the NLCE formalism for 1QP excitations and describe how the PCAT ensures that the effective Hamiltonian satisfies the required cluster-additivity property. Finally, we show how the 1QP dispersion relation is obtained from the effective Hamiltonian via Fourier transformation.

III.1 Block diagonalization

A quasiparticle ansatz typically characterizes the low-energy excitation spectrum by non-interacting dressed excitations. These correspond to block diagonalizing a strongly correlated many-body Hamiltonian into independent sectors labeled by quasiparticle number. Formally, given a Hamiltonian

H=H0+x​V,H=H_{0}+xV, (2)

with unperturbed part H0H_{0} and perturbation VV at strength xx, we seek to partition the Hilbert space into subspaces based on the number of elementary excitations above the ground state. The unperturbed Hamiltonian H0H_{0} is assumed to be exactly solvable and serves as the reference. Its eigenstates organize the Hilbert space into quasiparticle sectors. Denoting by E0[n]E_{0}^{[n]} the unperturbed energy of the nn quasiparticle subspace, the Hilbert space decomposes as

ℋ=⨁nℋ0[n].\mathcal{H}=\bigoplus_{n}\mathcal{H}_{0}^{[n]}. (3)

Each ℋ0[n]\mathcal{H}_{0}^{[n]} carries all states with eigenvalue E0[n]E_{0}^{[n]} of H0H_{0} corresponding to nn quasiparticles. We call H0H_{0} block diagonal if

H0=⨁n=0NH0[n​n]H_{0}=\bigoplus_{n=0}^{N}H_{0}^{[nn]} (4)

and H0[n​n]H_{0}^{[nn]} keeps ℋ0[n]\mathcal{H}_{0}^{[n]} invariant. We call a transformation UU block diagonalizing if

Heff=U†​H​U,H_{\mathrm{eff}}=U^{\dagger}HU, (5)

and HeffH_{\mathrm{eff}} retains the block structure of H0H_{0}, i.e.,

Heff=⨁n=0NHeff[n​n].H_{\mathrm{eff}}=\bigoplus_{n=0}^{N}H_{\mathrm{eff}}^{[nn]}. (6)

Here, Heff[n​n]H_{\mathrm{eff}}^{[nn]} denotes the block corresponding to the nn quasiparticle sector. For example, Heff[11]H_{\mathrm{eff}}^{[11]} is the N×NN\times N matrix for the 1QP block, where NN is the number of sites.

The subspace ℋeff[n]\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{eff}}^{{[n]}} is defined as containing those eigenstates of HH that adiabatically follow the states of ℋ0[n]\mathcal{H}_{0}^{[n]} as the perturbation strength x′x^{\prime} varies from 0 to xx in H=H0+x′​VH=H_{0}+x^{\prime}V.

In realistic settings, one can not block diagonalize the full Hamiltonian but only the low-energy part. In our case, we restrict the decomposition to three sectors consisting of the ground-state subspace ℋeff[0]\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{eff}}^{[0]}, the 1QP subspace ℋeff[1]\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{eff}}^{[1]}, and all higher excitations. The pictorial representation of such a block-diagonal Hamiltonian is shown in Fig. 2, where the block diagonalizing UU should eliminate the faint blue and green off-diagonal sectors Heff[n​m]H_{\mathrm{eff}}^{[nm]} with n≠mn\neq m.

A complete diagonalization of an infinite system is intractable, but LCEs provide a systematic approximation by combining results from finite clusters to recover thermodynamic-limit properties. For LCEs to converge, the transformation must be cluster additive: Disconnected clusters should contribute zero. However, even for the block-diagonalizing part of UU infinitely many choices exist for a degenerate subspace nn as discussed in Ref. [34]. While the ground state is uniquely determined, any unitary rotation within the 1QP subspace yields an equally valid block diagonalization due to the quasi-degeneracy. Higher-energy sectors have even more freedom.

This freedom necessitates, but also allows one to tailor the structure of the effective Hamiltonian to ensure cluster additivity. In particular, the PCAT [31] yields a specific unitary UPCATU_{\mathrm{PCAT}} that preserves cluster additivity. Cluster additivity ensures that only connected clusters need to be calculated, as disconnected clusters contribute zero, significantly reducing computational cost.

III.2 Linked-cluster expansions

In this subsection, we first outline the LCE framework assuming a suitable effective Hamiltonian exists, and then specify the requirements it must satisfy.

The general formalism for perturbative and nonperturbative LCEs is reviewed in Refs. [24, 27, 28]. First introduced for perturbative calculations of ground-state energies in quantum many-body systems, LCEs were subsequently extended to the study of excitation energies [25]. The core idea of LCEs is to decompose the lattice into topologically distinct, finite connected subgraphs called clusters CC, and use the inclusion-exclusion principle to sum up their additive contributions to recover thermodynamic-limit properties. Let us for the moment assume that the 1QP effective Hamiltonian Heff,C[1]H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},C} is such an additive quantity acting as a linear operator in the space of NN excitations. Then, the LCE scheme goes as follows.

A cluster is a finite set of sites connected by bonds, where sites carry on-site Hamiltonian terms (transverse and longitudinal fields) and bonds carry the two-body interactions (X​XXX couplings). These clusters are chosen with rectangular graph expansion having the dimensions Lm×Ln≤NmaxL_{m}\times L_{n}\leq N_{\mathrm{max}} where NmaxN_{\mathrm{max}}, is the maximum number of spins taken in NLCE calculation.

The reduced contribution of a cluster CC is defined recursively as

H¯eff,C[1]=Heff,C[1]−∑C′⊊CwC′/C​H¯eff,C′[1],\bar{H}^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},C}=H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},C}-\sum_{C^{\prime}\subsetneq C}w_{C^{\prime}/C}\,\bar{H}^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},C^{\prime}}, (7)

where wC′/Cw_{C^{\prime}/C} counts embeddings of the subgraph C′C^{\prime} inside CC. Summing the reduced contributions gives the effective 1QP Hamiltonian in the thermodynamic limit,

Heff[1]=∑CwC​H¯eff,C[1],H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff}}=\sum_{C}w_{C}\,\bar{H}^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},C}, (8)

where weight wCw_{C} counts embeddings of cluster CC per lattice site.

Often, one uses a full graph decomposition for the NLCE where the calculation is performed on topologically distinct graphs of minimal size. However, the number of graphs increases exponentially with the number of sites, which is challenging for the NLCE+VQE approach. As for the NLCE+VQE for ground-state energy [11], we adopt a rectangular graph expansion [35] for NLCE. In this expansion, only clusters of size Lm×LnL_{m}\times L_{n} with Lm⋅Ln≤NmaxL_{m}\cdot L_{n}\leq N_{\mathrm{max}} are included, where NmaxN_{\mathrm{max}} is the maximum number of spins in the largest cluster of the NLCE. These clusters have open boundary conditions. The rectangular graph expansion is applicable for the chain and the square lattice discussed below and is beneficial because the number of clusters increases polynomially with NN. For the one-dimensional chain, this reduces to considering open segments of length Lm≤NmaxL_{m}\leq N_{\mathrm{max}}. We will apply this expansion to the TFIM+LF in Sec. V. The rectangular graph expansion for the square lattice is illustrated in Fig. 3.

We now specify the calculation of Heff,C[1]H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},C} and how it can be made into a cluster-additive quantity. The effective 1QP Hamiltonian on a cluster CC with NN 1QP states is an N×NN\times N matrix defined as

Heff,C[1]=(U†​H​U)[11]−EC[0],H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},C}=(U^{\dagger}HU)^{[11]}-E^{[0]}_{C}, (9)

where [11] denotes the 1QP block and UU is the block-diagonalizing transformation. EC[0]E^{[0]}_{C} is obtained from the same VQE procedure: either via a separate ground-state minimization (separate-unitary case), or in the single-unitary case via diagonalization of the Hamiltonian projected onto the VQE-prepared subspace (see Sec. IV.3.2). The ground-state energy EC[0]E^{[0]}_{C} must be subtracted to ensure that Heff,C[1]H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},C} is intensive [25]. Importantly, since EC[0]E^{[0]}_{C} enters only as a diagonal shift of Heff,C[1]H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},C}, any estimation error from VQE affects only the on-site energies and leaves the hopping matrix elements unchanged. After Fourier transformation in the NLCE embedding, this propagates at most to a momentum-independent shift of ω⁡(k→)\omega(\vec{k}), leaving its shape and bandwidth unaffected.

The need for subtracting the ground-state energy is best understood through a concrete example. Consider two disconnected clusters AA and BB (i.e., they share no sites or bonds). Since the Hamiltonians HAH_{A} and HBH_{B} on the two disconnected clusters commute, [HA⊗𝟙B,𝟙A⊗HB]=0[H_{A}\otimes\mathds{1}_{B},\mathds{1}_{A}\otimes H_{B}]=0, it follows for the eigenfunctions on A∪BA\cup B that

|ΨA∪B[n+m]⟩=|ΨA[n]⟩⊗|ΨB[m]⟩.\ket{\Psi^{[n+m]}_{A\cup B}}\;=\;\ket{\Psi^{[n]}_{A}}\otimes\ket{\Psi^{[m]}_{B}}. (10)

Here, |Ψ[n]⟩|\Psi^{[n]}\rangle denotes an eigenstate of the full Hamiltonian HH with nn quasiparticles, and [n][n] ([m][m]) refers to the number of quasiparticles on cluster AA (BB). The effective Hamiltonian part on A∪BA\cup B that describes 1QP excitations within BB would always have a contribution of the ground-state energy on AA. Hence, one has to subtract it (n=0n=0 and m=1m=1 in the above formula).

This is linked to the concept of cluster additivity. A transformation UU is cluster-additive if

U†​HA∪B​U=Heff,A∪B=Heff,A⊗𝟙B+𝟙A⊗Heff,B.U^{\dagger}H_{A\cup B}U=H_{\mathrm{eff},A\cup B}=H_{\mathrm{eff},A}\otimes\mathds{1}_{B}+\mathds{1}_{A}\otimes H_{\mathrm{eff},B}. (11)

If fulfilled,

H¯eff,A∪B[1]=Heff,A∪B[1]−EA∪B[0]=H¯eff,A[1]⊕H¯eff,B[1]\bar{H}^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},A\cup B}\;=\;H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},A\cup B}-E^{[0]}_{A\cup B}\;=\;\bar{H}^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},A}\oplus\bar{H}^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},B} (12)

will hold. Subtracting the ground-state energy alone is necessary, but not sufficient to ensure cluster additivity.

In the next subsection, we explain how PCAT constructs a transformation UPCATU_{\mathrm{PCAT}} that guarantees both properties using only limited information from the ground-state and 1QP subspaces.

III.3 Projective cluster-additive transformation

In LCEs, both perturbative and nonperturbative, it is essential that observables on large systems can be consistently constructed from smaller, disconnected clusters. To understand why PCAT [31] achieves cluster additivity, we first establish the mathematical requirements.

Two clusters are disconnected if the unperturbed Hamiltonian is cluster additive on them (see Sec. III.2) [32]:

HA∪B=HA⊗𝟙B+𝟙A⊗HB.H_{A\cup B}\;=\;H_{A}\otimes\mathds{1}_{B}+\mathds{1}_{A}\otimes H_{B}. (13)

We demand of a transformation UU that when applied to the full Hamiltonian H=H0+x​VH\;=\;H_{0}+xV, U†​H​UU^{\dagger}HU^{\phantom{\dagger}} remains cluster additive on two disconnected clusters AA and BB. This ensures that no nonlinked clusters contribute to the expansion. We first illustrate why standard approaches fail to maintain cluster additivity, then show how PCAT resolves this issue through a modified state construction.

To understand that PCAT fulfills cluster additivity, we have to investigate the product state structure of eigenstates on A∪BA\cup B. Let {|Φi[n]⟩}\{\ket{\Phi^{[n]}_{i}}\} denote the eigenstates of H0H_{0} in the (n+1)(n+1)th subspace, and let {|Ψi[n]⟩}\{\ket{\Psi^{[n]}_{i}}\} denote the corresponding eigenstates of the full Hamiltonian HH, where ii labels states within the degenerate manifold. P[n]P^{[n]} is the corresponding projector, and P¯[n]\bar{P}^{[n]} the adiabatically connected projector of the full Hamiltonian HH. On A∪BA\cup B eigenstates have the product form as in Eq. 10.

It is instructive to see why a widely used approach to decouple an energy block fails to be cluster additive: The canonical two-block (2b) transformation (Schrieffer-Wolff, des Cloizeaux, Takahashi, etc. [24, 36, 34, 37, 38, 19]), which can be written in projector form for the transformation restricted to block nn as

U2​b[n]=P¯[n](P[n]P¯[n]P[n])−1/2,U^{[n]}_{\mathrm{2b}}=\bar{P}^{[n]}(P^{[n]}\bar{P}^{[n]}P^{[n]})^{-1/2}, (14)

where (M)−1/2(M)^{-1/2} for a rank-deficient matrix MM denotes the inverse square root restricted to the range of MM, or equivalently, the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse square root. This convention applies throughout this section whenever inverse operations are applied to projector products. The full transformation U2​b=∑nU2​b[n]U_{\mathrm{2b}}=\sum_{n}U_{\mathrm{2b}}^{[n]} minimizes ‖1−U2​b‖\|1-U_{\mathrm{2b}}\| . Let U[n]U^{[n]} denote the 2N×Nn2^{N}\times N_{n} matrix whose columns are the exact eigenvectors of HH corresponding to the nnth subspace, where NnN_{n} is the dimension of that subspace. When embedded in the full 2N×2N2^{N}\times 2^{N} space (as needed for sums like ∑nU[n]\sum_{n}U^{[n]}), this is understood as a partial isometry extended by zeros outside the nn-quasiparticle subspace. The transformation can also be given in terms of the overlap matrix X[n]X^{[n]}, an Nn×NnN_{n}\times N_{n} matrix with elements

Xi​j[n]=⟨Φi[n]|Ψj[n]⟩,X^{[n]}_{ij}=\langle\Phi^{[n]}_{i}|\Psi^{[n]}_{j}\rangle, (15)

where |Φi[n]⟩|\Phi^{[n]}_{i}\rangle are the unperturbed eigenstates and |Ψj[n]⟩|\Psi^{[n]}_{j}\rangle are the eigenstates of HH in block nn. Then,

U2​b[n]=U[n]X[n]†(X[n]X[n]†)−1/2.U_{2b}^{[n]}=U^{[n]}X^{[n]\dagger}(X^{[n]}X^{[n]\dagger})^{-1/2}. (16)

Written this way, the problem with cluster additivity becomes apparent: For simplicity, consider the 1QP excitations (n=1n=1). Then X[1]X^{[1]} becomes non-block-diagonal for disconnected clusters owing to the product form when the unperturbed ground state overlaps with excited states (i.e., P[1]​|Ψ[0]⟩≠0P^{[1]}\ket{\Psi^{[0]}}\neq 0). Contributions from |ΨA[0]⟩⊗|ΨB[1]⟩\ket{\Psi^{[0]}_{A}}\otimes\ket{\Psi^{[1]}_{B}} lead to nonzero elements in X[1]X^{[1]} at the same entries as |ΨA[1]⟩⊗|ΨB[0]⟩\ket{\Psi^{[1]}_{A}}\otimes\ket{\Psi^{[0]}_{B}}. This leads to intercluster matrix elements between blocks AA and BB. It also modifies matrix elements in the AA-only or BB-only blocks compared to the isolated AA and BB clusters.

Thus, cluster additivity is violated and dressed quasiparticles can hop between disconnected clusters (see Fig. 4). In the thermodynamic limit, disconnected clusters can be arbitrarily far apart, so such hopping represents unphysical infinite-range coupling. This artifact arises because the 2b transformation creates entanglement between clusters that should be independent.

In order to resolve this, PCAT [31] constructs modified states {|Ψ~[n]⟩}\{\,|\widetilde{\Psi}^{[n]}\rangle\} from the original eigenstates by eliminating all components projected onto lower-energy subspaces of H0H_{0}, using only subtractions of states from the low-energy spectrum. These modified states lie within the span of low-energy eigenspaces but are not eigenstates themselves. From these states, one constructs a modified overlap X~[n]\widetilde{X}^{[n]}, which in contrast to X[n]X^{[n]} is now block diagonal again on AA and BB. In detail, the construction of modified states goes as follows.

The recursion for constructing modified 1QP states is

|Ψ~[0]⟩=|Ψ[0]⟩,\displaystyle|\widetilde{\Psi}^{[0]}\rangle=|\Psi^{[0]}\rangle,
|Ψ~i[1]⟩=|Ψi[1]⟩−⟨Φ[0]|Ψi[1]⟩⟨Φ[0]|Ψ[0]⟩​|Ψ[0]⟩,\displaystyle|\widetilde{\Psi}^{[1]}_{i}\rangle=|\Psi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle-\frac{\langle\Phi^{[0]}|\Psi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle}{\langle\Phi^{[0]}|\Psi^{[0]}\rangle}|\Psi^{[0]}\rangle, (17)

which ensures that P[0]​|Ψ~i[1]⟩=0P^{[0]}|\widetilde{\Psi}^{[1]}_{i}\rangle=0 for all 1QP states. This removes any admixture of the ground state from the 1QP eigenstates. Note that in the special case where ⟨Φ[0]|Ψ[1]⟩=0\langle\Phi^{[0]}|\Psi^{[1]}\rangle=0 the transformation remains the same for the one-particle subspace. This is the case for the transverse-field Ising model, but as soon as the parity is broken, e.g., by a longitudinal field, the corrections become necessary.

For higher subspaces, the construction generalizes by recursively projecting out all unperturbed lower-energy subspaces. Using the low-energy projector

R[n]=∑m<nP[m]R^{[n]}=\sum_{m<n}P^{[m]} (18)

and its adiabatically connected counterpart R¯[n]\bar{R}^{[n]}, the general subtraction scheme reads

|Ψ~[n]⟩=(1−R¯[n]​(R[n]​R¯[n]​R[n])−1​R[n])​|Ψ[n]⟩.|\widetilde{\Psi}^{[n]}\rangle=\left(1-\bar{R}^{[n]}(R^{[n]}\bar{R}^{[n]}R^{[n]})^{-1}R^{[n]}\right)|\Psi^{[n]}\rangle. (19)

This ensures that each modified state |Ψ~[n]⟩|\widetilde{\Psi}^{[n]}\rangle has no projection onto lower-energy subspaces of H0H_{0}.

The key insight is that a state |ΨA∪B[n+m]⟩=|ΨA[n]⟩⊗|ΨB[m]⟩|\Psi^{[n+m]}_{A\cup B}\rangle=|\Psi^{[n]}_{A}\rangle\otimes|\Psi^{[m]}_{B}\rangle is transformed into

|Ψ~A∪B[n+m]⟩=|Ψ~A[n]⟩⊗|Ψ~B[m]⟩.|\widetilde{\Psi}^{[n+m]}_{A\cup B}\rangle=|\widetilde{\Psi}^{[n]}_{A}\rangle\otimes|\widetilde{\Psi}^{[m]}_{B}\rangle. (20)

This factorization is the essence of why PCAT preserves cluster additivity. Since modified states on A∪BA\cup B factor into modified states on AA and BB separately, the transformation introduces no artificial correlations between disconnected clusters. Each cluster’s quasiparticles remain localized on the cluster.

From this factorization property, several important consequences follow. In particular, it yields P[s]​|Ψ~A∪B[n+m]⟩=0P^{[s]}|\widetilde{\Psi}^{[n+m]}_{A\cup B}\rangle=0 for s<n+ms<n+m but also P[s]​|Ψ~A[n]⟩=0P^{[s]}|\widetilde{\Psi}^{[n]}_{A}\rangle=0 for s<ns<n and P[s]​|Ψ~B[m]⟩=0P^{[s]}|\widetilde{\Psi}^{[m]}_{B}\rangle=0 for s<ms<m. Indeed, the identity for modified states on disconnected clusters AA and BB is sufficient to guarantee cluster additivity of the transformation:

UPCAT†​HA∪B​UPCAT=Heff,A⊗𝟙B+𝟙A⊗Heff,B.U_{\mathrm{PCAT}}^{\dagger}H_{A\cup B}\,U_{\mathrm{PCAT}}^{\phantom{\dagger}}=H_{\mathrm{eff},A}\otimes\mathds{1}_{B}+\mathds{1}_{A}\otimes H_{\mathrm{eff},B}. (21)

We can now write the explicit form of the UPCATU_{\mathrm{PCAT}} transformation. The modified overlap matrix X~[n]\widetilde{X}^{[n]} is an Nn×NnN_{n}\times N_{n} matrix with elements

X~i​j[n]=⟨Ψi[n]|Ψ~j[n]⟩,\widetilde{X}^{[n]}_{ij}=\langle\Psi^{[n]}_{i}|\widetilde{\Psi}^{[n]}_{j}\rangle, (22)

where |Ψi[n]⟩|\Psi^{[n]}_{i}\rangle are the unperturbed eigenstates and |Ψ~j[n]⟩|\widetilde{\Psi}^{[n]}_{j}\rangle are the modified eigenstates in block nn. The transformation for a single block nn is then

UPCAT[n]=U[n]X~[n]†(X~[n]X~[n]†)−1/2,U_{\mathrm{PCAT}}^{[n]}=U^{[n]}\widetilde{X}^{[n]\dagger}(\widetilde{X}^{[n]}\widetilde{X}^{[n]\dagger})^{-1/2}, (23)

and for the full Hilbert space (with each block extended to 2N×2N2^{N}\times 2^{N} as partial isometries),

UPCAT=∑nUPCAT[n].U_{\mathrm{PCAT}}=\sum_{n}U_{\mathrm{PCAT}}^{[n]}. (24)

Since the modified states |Ψ~[n]⟩|\widetilde{\Psi}^{[n]}\rangle can be written using only projectors (as in the R[n]R^{[n]} form above), one can write UPCATU_{\mathrm{PCAT}} in terms of projectors only, which shows that it has a unique local perturbative expansion when using Kato’s perturbative series [39] for projection operators. This property implies that the transformation has the same form on every cluster. It enables a consistent perturbative expansion across clusters and ensures that a given perturbative order can be reached using the smallest possible clusters.

The projector form also establishes that the transformation satisfies

UPCAT[n]​(U[0],U[1],…,U[n])=UPCAT[n]​(U[0],…,U[n]​𝒲)U_{\mathrm{PCAT}}^{[n]}(U^{[0]},U^{[1]},\dots,U^{[n]})=U_{\mathrm{PCAT}}^{[n]}(U^{[0]},\dots,U^{[n]}\mathcal{W}) (25)

for arbitrary unitaries 𝒲∈𝒰⁡(Nn)\mathcal{W}\in\mathcal{U}(N_{n}) (the group of Nn×NnN_{n}\times N_{n} unitary matrices) acting within subspace nn, as rotations within a subspace do not affect the projection operators. This invariance property is essential for practical implementations.

Thus, PCAT yields a local, cluster-additive effective Hamiltonian built only from the low-energy eigenspaces and is compatible with both perturbative and nonperturbative LCEs.

This highlights the global character of the transformation; i.e., it can be fully constructed from the eigenspace of interest and those of lower energy. This global character is essential for our approach: VQE (Sec. IV) targets only the low-energy eigenspace, and PCAT constructs the transformation from this limited information, namely, energy expectations and state overlaps, without requiring knowledge of higher excitation sectors.

III.4 1QP dispersion in the thermodynamic limit

Once we obtain the effective Hamiltonian for finite clusters, the goal is to obtain the effective 1QP Hamiltonian and therefore the 1QP dispersion in the thermodynamic limit. For translationally invariant systems, 1QP eigenstates are labeled by momentum k→\vec{k}. With lattice spacing set to unity and assuming a single-site unit cell, the Brillouin zone is k∈[−π,π]k\in[-\pi,\pi] for the one-dimensional chain and k→=(kx,ky)∈[−π,π]2\vec{k}=(k_{x},k_{y})\in[-\pi,\pi]^{2} for the square lattice.

For this purpose, the rectangular clusters are embedded into the infinite lattice as explained in Sec. III.2 using the inclusion-exclusion principle. For the rectangular expansion, the embedding weight wCw_{C} for a cluster of size Lm×LnL_{m}\times L_{n} on an infinite lattice is simply unity (one embedding per lattice site in the thermodynamic limit). For translationally invariant models, eigenstates are also momentum eigenstates and Fourier transforming the real-space Hamiltonian gives the 1QP energies. The dispersion relation for both the chain and square lattice reads

ω⁡(k→)=∑Lm,Ln∑μ→,ν→exp⁡(i​k→⋅(ν→−μ→))​H¯eff,Lm×Ln,μ→,ν→[1],\omega(\vec{k})=\sum_{L_{m},L_{n}}\sum_{\vec{\mu},\vec{\nu}}\exp\big(i\vec{k}\cdot(\vec{\nu}-\vec{\mu})\big)\bar{H}^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},L_{m}\times L_{n},\vec{\mu},\vec{\nu}}\,, (26)

where μ→,ν→\vec{\mu},\vec{\nu} label lattice sites within the cluster. For the one-dimensional chain, Ln=1L_{n}=1 and k→\vec{k} reduces to scalar momentum kk. For the square lattice, k→=(kx,ky)\vec{k}=(k_{x},k_{y}) spans the two-dimensional Brillouin zone.
The calculation of reduced contribution is particularly simple for the rectangular expansion. It is easy to see that the contribution H¯eff,Lm×Ln,k→[1]\bar{H}^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},L_{m}\times L_{n},\vec{k}} of a cluster in kk space can be rewritten in terms of non-reduced contributions in the following way:

H¯eff,Lm×Ln,k→[1]\displaystyle\bar{H}^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},L_{m}\times L_{n},\vec{k}} =Heff,Lm×Ln,k→[1]\displaystyle=H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},L_{m}\times L_{n},\vec{k}} (27)
−2​Heff,Lm−1×Ln,k→[1]−2​Heff,Lm×Ln−1,k→[1]\displaystyle-2H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},L_{m}-1\times L_{n},\vec{k}}-2H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},L_{m}\times L_{n}-1,\vec{k}}
+4​Heff,Lm−1×Ln−1,k→[1]\displaystyle+4H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},L_{m}-1\times L_{n}-1,\vec{k}}
+Heff,Lm−2×Ln,k→[1]+Heff,Lm×Ln−2,k→[1]\displaystyle+H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},L_{m}-2\times L_{n},\vec{k}}+H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},L_{m}\times L_{n}-2,\vec{k}}
−2​Heff,Lm−1×Ln−2,k→[1]−2​Heff,Lm−2×Ln−1,k→[1]\displaystyle-2H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},L_{m}-1\times L_{n}-2,\vec{k}}-2H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},L_{m}-2\times L_{n}-1,\vec{k}}
+Heff,Lm−2×Ln−2,k→[1].\displaystyle+H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},L_{m}-2\times L_{n}-2,\vec{k}}\,.

The coefficients in this expression and the alternating signs follow from the inclusion-exclusion principle applied to rectangular geometry.

Each subtracted term removes overcounting from smaller clusters. This identity reveals an important insight: Only the largest clusters and their boundaries contribute to the rectangular expansion, as interior contributions cancel in the inclusion-exclusion sum. This property reduces error accumulation. Specifically, once clusters of size Lm×LnL_{m}\times L_{n} are included in the expansion, all clusters of size (Lm−2)×(Ln−2)(L_{m}-2)\times(L_{n}-2) or smaller have reduced contributions that vanish identically. Their physics is therefore fully captured by the larger embeddings. This is analogous to the 1D case where only clusters of size NN and N−1N-1 contribute to the dispersion at order Nmax=NN_{\mathrm{max}}=N.

Having established the NLCE framework, we now describe how VQE is used as the cluster solver.

IV VQE as cluster solver

The VQE is a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm for near-term quantum devices. In this section, we describe how VQE serves as the cluster solver within our NLCE framework, block-diagonalizing the Hamiltonian on each finite cluster to decouple the ground state and 1QP subspace from higher excitations.

As discussed in Sec. III.3, the unitary transformation UVQEU_{\mathrm{VQE}} obtained from VQE optimization alone is generally not cluster additive and therefore not suitable for direct use in NLCE. Instead, VQE provides the information, namely, the low-energy eigenspaces and their overlaps with the unperturbed states, needed to construct the cluster-additive transformation UPCATU_{\mathrm{PCAT}} via the PCAT scheme. From the full effective Hamiltonian Heff=UPCAT†​H​UPCATH_{\mathrm{eff}}=U_{\mathrm{PCAT}}^{\dagger}\,H\,U_{\mathrm{PCAT}}, we extract the 1QP block

Heff[1]=(UPCAT†​H​UPCAT)[11]−E[0],H_{\mathrm{eff}}^{[1]}=(U_{\mathrm{PCAT}}^{\dagger}\,H\,U_{\mathrm{PCAT}})^{[11]}-E^{[0]}, (28)

where the superscript [11] denotes the 1QP block and E[0]E^{[0]} is the ground-state energy.

A key advantage of the PCAT approach is that it requires only energy expectation values and overlaps, quantities that VQE can provide, rather than full state tomography, which would be exponentially costly. This efficiency stems from the structure of PCAT itself, as detailed in Sec. III.3.

Throughout the paper, we use VQE as cluster solver, though the PCAT framework is algorithm agnostic and applies equally to other eigenstate preparation methods such as quantum phase estimation or adiabatic state preparation.

VQE operates by minimizing a cost function C⁡(θ)C(\theta) that depends on variational parameters θ\theta characterizing a quantum circuit UVQE​(θ)U_{\mathrm{VQE}}(\theta). For ground-state calculations, the cost function is simply the energy expectation value, and the Rayleigh-Ritz variational principle ensures convergence to the lowest-energy state. For excited states, the situation is more subtle. Several approaches exist within the VQE framework for accessing excited states, including deflation methods [14], purified state approaches [17], and subspace-search methods [16]. Deflation methods sequentially compute excited states by enforcing orthogonality with previously found states. Purified state and subspace-search methods treat entire degenerate subspaces simultaneously, which is more natural for our purpose where we need to decouple a full quasidegenerate 1QP subspace on finite clusters.

The performance of VQE depends on two components: (1) the cost function, which must be designed to achieve block diagonalization rather than simply finding individual eigenstates, and (2) the ansatz for the variational circuit UVQE​(θ)U_{\mathrm{VQE}}(\theta), which must be sufficiently expressive yet trainable. For the ansatz, we adopt the HVA, which we successfully employed for ground-state energy calculations in our previous NLCE+VQE work [11]. The HVA is also well suited for excited states. Since the eigenstates of the full Hamiltonian are superpositions across multiple bare quasiparticle sectors of H0H_{0}, the ansatz must generate inter-sector mixing. The HVA achieves this naturally, as it is constructed directly from the terms of HH.

The remainder of this section is organized as follows. In Sec. IV.1, we discuss the design of cost functions for block diagonalization, introducing both variance-based and trace-based approaches and comparing their properties. In Sec. IV.2, we describe the HVA ansatz and our initialization strategy. Finally, in Sec. IV.3, we detail the quantum measurement protocol required to construct PCAT. This subsection describes how to extract energy expectations and state overlaps from the VQE solution and presents the explicit algorithm for computing UPCATU_{\mathrm{PCAT}}.

IV.1 Cost functions

For clarity, all cost functions below are evaluated on a finite cluster CC within the NLCE, though we suppress the cluster label for notational simplicity. The unitary UU appearing in the cost functions defined in this section is generic and can be realized by any ansatz.

VQE aims to find the parameters θ\theta that minimize a cost function C⁡(θ)C(\theta). For ground states, the ground-state energy EC[0]E^{[0]}_{C} can be obtained separately by direct energy minimization via the Rayleigh-Ritz principle,

CGS​(θ)=⟨Φ[0]|U†​(θ)​H​U​(θ)|Φ[0]⟩,C^{\mathrm{GS}}(\theta)=\langle\Phi^{[0]}|\,U^{\dagger}(\theta)\,H\,U(\theta)|\Phi^{[0]}\rangle, (29)

or jointly as part of the combined GS+1QP cost functions described below for ground state and excited states.

IV.1.1 Variance-based cost functions

One effective approach is to minimize the energy variance [40, 41], ⟨H2⟩−⟨H⟩2\langle H^{2}\rangle-\langle H\rangle^{2}. For a state |Ψ⟩=∑ncn​|ϕn⟩|\Psi\rangle=\sum_{n}c_{n}|\phi_{n}\rangle expanded in the eigenbasis of HH with eigenvalues EnE_{n}, the variance equals ∑n|cn|2​(En−E¯)2\sum_{n}|c_{n}|^{2}(E_{n}-\bar{E})^{2}, where E¯=∑n|cn|2​En\bar{E}=\sum_{n}|c_{n}|^{2}E_{n} is the energy expectation value and the sum runs over energy eigenstates. The variance vanishes if and only if the state lies within a single energy eigenspace. For nondegenerate spectra, this requires an eigenstate; for degenerate subspaces, any superposition within the degenerate manifold yields zero variance. This quantity measures the extent to which HH has been block diagonalized and is related to residual off-diagonal elements in the context of continuous unitary transformations.

To decouple a quasidegenerate 1QP subspace from the rest of the spectrum, we generalize to multiple states. For a set of 1QP basis states {|Φi[1]⟩}i=1N\{|\Phi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle\}_{i=1}^{N} transformed by unitary U⁡(θ)U(\theta), the variance cost function is

Cvar1​Q​P​(θ)\displaystyle C_{\mathrm{var}}^{1\mathrm{QP}}(\theta) =\displaystyle= ∑i=1N⟨Φi[1]|U†​(θ)​H2​U​(θ)|Φi[1]⟩\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{N}\langle\Phi^{[1]}_{i}|\,U^{\dagger}(\theta)\,H^{2}\,U(\theta)|\Phi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle (30)
−\displaystyle- ∑i,j=1N|⟨Φi[1]|U†​(θ)​H​U​(θ)|Φj[1]⟩|2.\displaystyle\sum_{i,j=1}^{N}\bigl|\langle\Phi^{[1]}_{i}|\,U^{\dagger}(\theta)\,H\,U(\theta)|\Phi^{[1]}_{j}\rangle\bigr|^{2}\,.

This cost function is unitarily invariant within the 1QP subspace: Any rotation of the basis {|Φi[1]⟩}\{|\Phi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle\} by a unitary acting only within this subspace leaves Cvar1​Q​PC^{\mathrm{1QP}}_{\mathrm{var}} unchanged. Physically, this means the cost function enforces block-diagonalization (decoupling the 1QP subspace from other sectors) without requiring full diagonalization within the 1QP block itself; the internal structure of the block remains flexible. In contrast, minimizing the variance for each state individually (as done in Ref. [41]) would not preserve this unitary invariance in the full subspace. The residual variance after optimization directly indicates the quality of decoupling achieved.

We can use variance-based cost functions in two ways. Either optimize Cvar1​Q​PC_{\mathrm{var}}^{\mathrm{1QP}} alone for the 1QP sector (with a separate ground-state calculation using energy minimization) or include both sectors simultaneously:

CvarGS,1​Q​P​(θ)\displaystyle C^{\mathrm{GS,1QP}}_{\mathrm{var}}(\theta) =\displaystyle= ⟨Φ[0]|U†​(θ)​H2​U​(θ)|Φ[0]⟩\displaystyle\langle\Phi^{[0]}|\,U^{\dagger}(\theta)\,H^{2}\,U(\theta)|{\Phi^{[0]}}\rangle (31)
−\displaystyle- |⟨Φ[0]|U†​(θ)​H​U​(θ)|Φ[0]⟩|2+Cvar1​Q​P​(θ),\displaystyle|\langle\Phi^{[0]}|\,U^{\dagger}(\theta)\,H\,U(\theta)|{\Phi^{[0]}}\rangle|^{2}+C^{\mathrm{1QP}}_{\mathrm{var}}(\theta),

where |Φ[0]⟩|\Phi^{[0]}\rangle is the ground state of the unperturbed Hamiltonian H0H_{0}. We use equal weights (coefficient 1) for both the ground-state variance and the 1QP variance, treating both sectors symmetrically. Unlike the trace cost function (discussed below), which is unitarily invariant in the combined (GS+1QP) space, this sum has separate unitary invariances in each subspace. This has the advantage that minimizing variance in each sector separately actively drives orthogonality between the ground-state and 1QP subspace. Perfect optimization (zero variance) guarantees orthogonality; in practice, finite residual variance can reflect approximate orthogonality with the degree of mixing controlled by the residual.

IV.1.2 Trace-based cost functions

An alternative approach minimizes the sum of weighted energies [16]:

CtrGS,1​Q​P​(θ)\displaystyle C^{\mathrm{GS,1QP}}_{\mathrm{tr}}(\theta) =\displaystyle= w0​⟨Φ[0]|​U†​(θ)​H​U​(θ)​|Φ[0]⟩\displaystyle w_{0}\langle\Phi^{[0]}|\,U^{\dagger}(\theta)\,H\,U(\theta)|\Phi^{[0]}\rangle (32)
+\displaystyle+ ∑i=1Nwi​⟨Φi[1]|​U†​(θ)​H​U​(θ)​|Φi[1]⟩.\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{N}w_{i}\langle\Phi^{[1]}_{i}|\,U^{\dagger}(\theta)\,H\,U(\theta)|\Phi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle.

We use uniform weights w0=wi=1w_{0}=w_{i}=1 for all ii, making the cost function basis invariant. It is thus the trace over the combined ground-state and 1QP subspace. This is natural for linked-cluster expansions where we require the full subspace information and treat all sites equivalently. We apply this trace cost function in two ways: Ctr1​Q​PC_{\mathrm{tr}}^{\mathrm{1QP}} targets only the 1QP sector [w0=0w_{0}=0 in Eq. (32) and separate ground-state optimization], while CtrGS,1​Q​PC_{\mathrm{tr}}^{\mathrm{GS,1QP}} treats both ground-state and 1QP subspace with a single unitary.

The trace minimization is motivated by the fact that block diagonalization preserves the sum of eigenvalues within each block. However, when ground and excited states are included together, minimizing the trace does not guarantee that U⁡(θ)​|Φ[0]⟩U(\theta)|\Phi^{[0]}\rangle is the true lowest-energy state. A postprocessing diagonalization step (described in Sec. IV.3) is therefore required to identify the actual ground state and extract 1QP energies.

The trace cost function can also be evaluated using a purified approach where the whole subspace is treated as a wavefunction in a larger Hilbert space [17, 18].

IV.1.3 Comparison and choice

We distinguish between two different implementation strategies. With single-unitary approaches (CtrGS,1​Q​PC_{\mathrm{tr}}^{\mathrm{GS,1QP}}, CvarGS,1​Q​PC_{\mathrm{var}}^{\mathrm{GS,1QP}}), orthogonality is preserved throughout optimization by construction. However, CtrGS,1​Q​PC_{\mathrm{tr}}^{\mathrm{GS,1QP}} requires postprocessing diagonalization to identify the true ground state, while CvarGS,1​Q​PC_{\mathrm{var}}^{\mathrm{GS,1QP}} directly yields approximate eigenstates. With the separate-unitary approach (Cvar1​Q​PC_{\mathrm{var}}^{\mathrm{1QP}}), orthogonality must be verified and may require a generalized eigenvalue problem when non-orthogonality occurs.

We tested both strategies across all models studied in Sec. V. For the pure TFIM cases, all cost functions achieve similar convergence and stability, successfully decoupling the low-energy block. The trace-based approach requires fewer measurements, as it only needs energy expectation values ⟨H⟩\langle H\rangle, while variance-based approaches additionally require ⟨H2⟩\langle H^{2}\rangle measurements. Variance-based approaches provide residual variance as a diagnostic for block-diagonalization quality. However, for TFIM+LF where parity breaking makes optimization more challenging, trace-based cost functions show greater robustness to ground-state initialization, while variance-based approaches require near-zero initialization for larger clusters (see Sec. V.2).

The variance-based approach Cvar1​Q​PC_{\mathrm{var}}^{\mathrm{1QP}} has the additional flexibility of applying only to the excitation sector with separate ground-state calculation. However, with separate unitaries, orthogonality between ground-state and 1QP subspace is not enforced during optimization and must be verified. The other two cost functions (CtrGS,1​Q​PC_{\mathrm{tr}}^{\mathrm{GS,1QP}} and CvarGS,1​Q​PC_{\mathrm{var}}^{\mathrm{GS,1QP}}) maintain orthogonality throughout optimization via their single-unitary structure. The residual value of CvarC_{\mathrm{var}} directly quantifies block-diagonalization quality, making it useful for convergence monitoring.

IV.2 State preparation

The performance of VQE depends on the ansatz choice, which must balance expressibility and trainability. The HVA [33] provides this balance by incorporating the problem structure directly into the circuit design. Motivated by quantum approximate optimization algorithm [42] and adiabatic quantum computing [43], HVA is formulated based on the structure of the Hamiltonian under investigation and has been successfully applied for ground-state calculations in quantum many-body systems [33, 6, 44, 45, 46, 47].

IV.2.1 Hamiltonian variational ansatz

Our recent work [11] investigated HVA performance for ground-state energy calculations. Here, we employ HVA to minimize the cost functions in Eqs. (30) and (32) that block diagonalize the Hamiltonian. For a Hamiltonian decomposed as H=∑μHμH=\sum_{\mu}H_{\mu}, the HVA unitary takes the form

UHVA​(θ)=∏l(∏μei​θl,μ​Hμ),U_{\mathrm{HVA}}(\theta)=\prod_{l}\big(\prod_{\mu}e^{\mathrm{i}\theta_{l,\mu}H_{\mu}}\big), (33)

where ll indexes the layers. The HVA construction follows the physical intuition of adiabatic evolution: Each layer implements a discrete evolution step alternating between the unperturbed Hamiltonian H0H_{0} and the perturbation VV, with variational parameters that can transform the unperturbed eigenstates into eigenstates of the full Hamiltonian H=H0+x​VH=H_{0}+xV. Following the bang-bang digitized adiabatic approach [44], we group commuting terms together and separate non-commuting terms to create blocks that are individually classically solvable, thereby minimizing Trotter error.

For the TFIM+LF [Eq. (1)] on any cluster graph CC, the HVA unitary is:

UHVA,C​(θ)=∏l=1Nlei​∑νθν,lZ​Zν⋅ei​∑νθν,lX​Xν⋅ei​∑⟨ν,μ⟩θν,μ,lX​X​Xν​Xμ.U_{\mathrm{HVA},\,C}(\theta)=\prod_{l=1}^{N_{l}}e^{\mathrm{i}\sum_{\nu}\theta^{Z}_{\nu,l}Z_{\nu}}\cdot e^{\mathrm{i}\sum_{\nu}\theta^{X}_{\nu,l}X_{\nu}}\cdot e^{\mathrm{i}\sum_{\langle\nu,\mu\rangle}\theta^{XX}_{\nu,\mu,l}X_{\nu}X_{\mu}}. (34)

The X​X−X−ZXX-X-Z ordering exemplifies this strategy: Since [Xν​Xμ,Xρ]=0[X_{\nu}X_{\mu},X_{\rho}]=0, the X​XXX-coupling and XX-field blocks commute and are placed adjacently, forming HX​X−X=−∑⟨ν,μ⟩XνXμ−hX∑νXνH_{XX-X}=-\sum_{\langle\nu,\mu\rangle}X_{\nu}X_{\mu}-h_{X}\sum_{\nu}X_{\nu}, which is classically solvable (eigenstates are product states in the XX basis). The ZZ-field block HZ=−hZ∑νZνH_{Z}=-h_{Z}\sum_{\nu}Z_{\nu} is also diagonal. This creates two classically solvable parts per layer. On a cluster of NN spins, each HVA layer requires NN qubits, 2​N2N single-qubit rotations (NN for the ZZ block and NN for the XX block), and one two-qubit gate per nearest-neighbor bond from the X​XXX block (N−1N-1 for an open one-dimensional chain). This layer structure is illustrated in Fig. 5 for the one-dimensional case. The general principle of grouping commuting terms to form classically solvable blocks applies to arbitrary cluster geometries.

We emphasize that the presence of symmetries allows for parameter reduction. Symmetries of the Hamiltonian translate into symmetries of the optimal unitary, constraining the variational parameters. If [H,𝒮]=0[H,\mathcal{S}]=0 for symmetry operation 𝒮\mathcal{S}, then any block-diagonalizing unitary UU can be chosen to commute with 𝒮\mathcal{S}, imposing parameter constraints. For the one-dimensional chain, reflection symmetry about the center implies θiq=θN+1−iq\theta^{q}_{i}=\theta^{q}_{N+1-i} (where qq labels the parameter type), reducing parameters by roughly half. For NLCE, most clusters have only discrete symmetries (reflection, rotation); periodic chains additionally have translational invariance allowing further reduction.

IV.2.2 Initialization strategy

Good initialization is crucial for successful optimization. We employ a two-stage protocol. All qubits are initialized in the computational basis state |0⟩|0\rangle, denoted as |ref⟩|\mathrm{ref}\rangle. For the high-field polarized phase of the TFIM, this coincides with the unperturbed ground state |Φ[0]⟩|\Phi^{[0]}\rangle of H0H_{0}. The initial parameters θinitial\theta_{\mathrm{initial}} determine the starting configuration via UHVA​(θinitial)​|ref⟩U_{\mathrm{HVA}}(\theta_{\mathrm{initial}})|\mathrm{ref}\rangle.

Stage 1 We first optimize UHVA​(θ)U_{\mathrm{HVA}}(\theta) for the ground state alone by minimizing energy expectation value (not variance), ensuring convergence to the lowest-energy state via the Rayleigh-Ritz variational principle. Initializing all parameters to small values close to zero ensures reliable convergence.

Stage 2 We use the optimized ground-state parameters θGS\theta_{\mathrm{GS}} as initialization for optimizing the full subspace cost functions:

UHVA​(θ)​Xi​|ref⟩=UHVA​(θ)​Xi​UHVA​(θGS)†​UHVA​(θGS)​|ref⟩,U_{\mathrm{HVA}}(\theta)X_{i}|\mathrm{ref}\rangle=U_{\mathrm{HVA}}(\theta)X_{i}U_{\mathrm{HVA}}(\theta_{\mathrm{GS}})^{\dagger}U_{\mathrm{HVA}}(\theta_{\mathrm{GS}})|\mathrm{ref}\rangle, (35)

where Xi​|ref⟩X_{i}|\mathrm{ref}\rangle form the 1QP basis of H0H_{0}. If the ground-state unitary provides a good approximation to the true ground state, then UHVA​(θGS)​Xi​UHVA​(θGS)†U_{\mathrm{HVA}}(\theta_{\mathrm{GS}})X_{i}U_{\mathrm{HVA}}(\theta_{\mathrm{GS}})^{\dagger} acts as an approximate excitation operator. For the one-dimensional TFIM, this initialization already provides nearly exact 1QP states, requiring minimal further optimization. For two-dimensional TFIM and models with longitudinal field, the initialization provides a good starting point that improves convergence compared to random parametrization, though substantial optimization is still required to achieve accurate decoupling.

The ground-state solution provides a physics-informed initialization strategy that leverages the already-optimized ground-state parameters. This approach reflects warm-start principles, beginning optimization with lower initial cost function values compared to random initialization, and proves effective in most cases. However, as we show in Secs. V.1.2 and V.2, it can lead to local minima for variance-based cost functions when optimizing larger clusters, while trace-based approaches remain robust. In cases where convergence issues arise, initializing parameters near zero provides more stable convergence despite starting with higher initial cost function values.

IV.3 Quantum circuit implementation and measurement requirements

Once VQE optimization is complete and we have obtained the optimized parameters θopt\theta_{\mathrm{opt}}, we must perform additional quantum measurements to extract the information needed for constructing the PCAT unitary UPCATU_{\mathrm{PCAT}} and the effective 1QP Hamiltonian Heff[1]H_{\mathrm{eff}}^{[1]}. As discussed in Sec. III.3, PCAT requires constructing modified states that eliminate projections onto lower-energy subspaces of H0H_{0}. Since VQE provides a unitary transformation UVQEU_{\mathrm{VQE}} rather than explicit state vectors, we must extract the necessary information through quantum measurements.

We organize this procedure into two parts: Sec. IV.3.1 describes the quantum measurements required to obtain three essential (N+1)×(N+1)(N+1)\times(N+1) matrices (𝒪\mathcal{O}, SS, H~\tilde{H}), and Sec. IV.3.2 describes the classical postprocessing steps to construct UPCATU_{\mathrm{PCAT}} and extract Heff[1]H_{\mathrm{eff}}^{[1]}.

IV.3.1 Quantum measurements

After VQE optimization yields optimal parameters θopt\theta_{\mathrm{opt}}, we have a set of N+1N+1 VQE-prepared states that approximately span the ground-state and 1QP subspace. We label the VQE-prepared ground state as |χ[0]⟩|\chi^{[0]}\rangle and the VQE-prepared 1QP states as |χi[1]⟩|\chi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle for i=1,…,Ni=1,\ldots,N. We use χ\chi to denote VQE-prepared states, reserving Ψ\Psi for exact eigenstates. Here, UVQE[0]=UHVA​(θGS)U^{[0]}_{\mathrm{VQE}}=U_{\mathrm{HVA}}(\theta_{\mathrm{GS}}) and UVQE[1]=UHVA​(θ1​Q​P)U^{[1]}_{\mathrm{VQE}}=U_{\mathrm{HVA}}(\theta_{\mathrm{1QP}}), where θGS\theta_{\mathrm{GS}} and θ1​Q​P\theta_{\mathrm{1QP}} are the optimized parameters for ground state and excited states. UVQE[0,1]=UHVA​(θGS,1​Q​P)U^{[0,1]}_{\mathrm{VQE}}=U_{\mathrm{HVA}}(\theta_{\mathrm{GS,1QP}}) is used for the common unitary obtained after the optimization of the cost functions in Eqs.( 31) and ( 32).

How these states are prepared depends on the cost function used:

  • •

    For CtrGS,1​Q​PC^{\mathrm{GS,1QP}}_{\mathrm{tr}} or CvarGS,1​Q​PC_{\mathrm{var}}^{\mathrm{GS,1QP}} (single unitary): All states use the same optimized unitary: |χ[0]⟩=UVQE[0,1]​|Φ[0]⟩|\chi^{[0]}\rangle=U^{[0,1]}_{\mathrm{VQE}}|\Phi^{[0]}\rangle, |χi[1]⟩=UVQE[0,1]​|Φi[1]⟩|\chi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle=U^{[0,1]}_{\mathrm{VQE}}|\Phi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle, where |Φ[0]⟩|\Phi^{[0]}\rangle is the unperturbed ground state (which equals |ref⟩|\mathrm{ref}\rangle for our models) and |Φi[1]⟩=Xi​|ref⟩|\Phi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle=X_{i}|\mathrm{ref}\rangle are the unperturbed 1QP states.

  • •

    For Cvar1​Q​PC_{\mathrm{var}}^{\mathrm{1QP}} with separate ground-state optimization: We use different unitaries: |χ[0]⟩=UVQE[0]​|Φ[0]⟩|\chi^{[0]}\rangle=U^{[0]}_{\mathrm{VQE}}|\Phi^{[0]}\rangle, |χi[1]⟩=UVQE[1]​|Φi[1]⟩|\chi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle=U^{[1]}_{\mathrm{VQE}}|\Phi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle.

The three essential (N+1)×(N+1)(N+1)\times(N+1) matrices we must measure are:

Matrix 𝒪\mathcal{O} (overlap with unperturbed states) This (N+1)×(N+1)(N+1)\times(N+1) matrix contains overlaps between VQE-prepared states (rows) and unperturbed eigenstates |Φj[0]⟩|\Phi^{[0]}_{j}\rangle (columns, j∈{0,1,…,N}j\in\{0,1,\ldots,N\}). The ground-state row is 𝒪0​j=⟨χ[0]|Φj[0]⟩\mathcal{O}_{0j}=\langle\chi^{[0]}|\Phi^{[0]}_{j}\rangle, and the 1QP rows are 𝒪i​j=⟨χi[1]|Φj[0]⟩\mathcal{O}_{ij}=\langle\chi^{[1]}_{i}|\Phi^{[0]}_{j}\rangle for i=1,…,Ni=1,\ldots,N.

Matrix SS (overlap between VQE-prepared states) This matrix contains overlaps between the VQE-prepared states themselves. Elements are S00=⟨χ[0]|χ[0]⟩S_{00}=\langle\chi^{[0]}|\chi^{[0]}\rangle, S0​i=⟨χ[0]|χi[1]⟩S_{0i}=\langle\chi^{[0]}|\chi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle, and Si​j=⟨χi[1]|χj[1]⟩S_{ij}=\langle\chi^{[1]}_{i}|\chi^{[1]}_{j}\rangle.

For single-unitary cost functions, S=𝟙N+1S=\mathds{1}_{N+1} exactly (diagonal by construction). For separate-unitary approaches, off-diagonal elements S0​i=⟨χ[0]|χi[1]⟩S_{0i}=\langle\chi^{[0]}|\chi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle will be nonzero (unless there is an additional symmetry as in the pure TFIM), reflecting imperfect orthogonality.

Matrix H~\tilde{H} (Hamiltonian expectation values) This matrix contains Hamiltonian matrix elements in the basis of VQE-prepared states. Elements are H~00=⟨χ[0]|H|χ[0]⟩\tilde{H}_{00}=\langle\chi^{[0]}|H|\chi^{[0]}\rangle, H~0​i=⟨χ[0]|H|χi[1]⟩\tilde{H}_{0i}=\langle\chi^{[0]}|H|\chi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle, and H~i​j=⟨χi[1]|H|χj[1]⟩\tilde{H}_{ij}=\langle\chi^{[1]}_{i}|H|\chi^{[1]}_{j}\rangle.

The overlap matrix 𝒪\mathcal{O} and (when needed) the overlap matrix SS are measured using the Hadamard test [48]. The Hamiltonian matrix H~\tilde{H} can be measured more directly: Diagonal elements H~00\tilde{H}_{00} and H~i​i\tilde{H}_{ii} are expectation values obtained via standard Pauli measurements, while off-diagonal elements can be measured as expectation values on superposition states when both states are prepared using the same unitary. Specifically, by preparing superposition states such as |χ±⟩=(|χ[0]⟩±|χi[1]⟩)/2|\chi_{\pm}\rangle=(|\chi^{[0]}\rangle\pm|\chi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle)/\sqrt{2} or (|χi[1]⟩±|χj[1]⟩)/2(|\chi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle\pm|\chi^{[1]}_{j}\rangle)/\sqrt{2} and measuring ⟨H⟩\langle H\rangle, one obtains the real part of the off-diagonal elements; the imaginary part is obtained similarly using complex superpositions.

For separate-unitary approaches, overlaps and Hamiltonian matrix elements that couple different unitaries require the Hadamard test with composite unitaries. For example, S0​i=⟨χ[0]|χi[1]⟩=⟨Φ[0]|UVQE[0]†UVQE[1]|Φi[1]⟩S_{0i}=\langle\chi^{[0]}|\chi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle=\langle\Phi^{[0]}|U_{\mathrm{VQE}}^{[0]\dagger}U^{[1]}_{\mathrm{VQE}}|\Phi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle requires Hadamard test. Similarly, Hamiltonian expectation values coupling different unitaries, such as H~0​i=⟨χ[0]|H|χi[1]⟩=⟨Φ[0]|UVQE[0]†HUVQE[1]|Φi[1]⟩\tilde{H}_{0i}=\langle\chi^{[0]}|H|\chi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle=\langle\Phi^{[0]}|U_{\mathrm{VQE}}^{[0]\dagger}HU^{[1]}_{\mathrm{VQE}}|\Phi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle, also require Hadamard tests with composite unitaries. Within the 1QP block using the same unitary, H~i​j=⟨χi[1]|H|χj[1]⟩\tilde{H}_{ij}=\langle\chi^{[1]}_{i}|H|\chi^{[1]}_{j}\rangle can use superposition state measurements.

The total number of measurements scales as O⁡(N2)O(N^{2}) for each matrix. However, these measurements are performed only once after VQE optimization is complete, so they do not represent the computational bottleneck; the iterative VQE optimization itself is far more resource demanding.

IV.3.2 Classical postprocessing

Having obtained the three matrices 𝒪\mathcal{O}, SS, and H~\tilde{H} from quantum measurements, we now proceed entirely classically to construct UPCAT[1]U_{\mathrm{PCAT}}^{[1]} and extract Heff[1]H_{\mathrm{eff}}^{[1]}. This construction proceeds in four steps.

Step 1: Identify the true ground state and handle non-orthogonality.

When using CtrGS,1​Q​PC^{\mathrm{GS,1QP}}_{\mathrm{tr}}, the optimization does not guarantee that the nominal ground state |χ[0]⟩|\chi^{[0]}\rangle is the true lowest-energy eigenstate. When using separate unitaries (Cvar1​Q​PC_{\mathrm{var}}^{\mathrm{1QP}}), there may be non-zero overlaps S0​i≠0S_{0i}\neq 0 between ground and 1QP states. In both cases, we must solve an eigenvalue problem to find orthogonal eigenstates.

For single-unitary cases where S=𝟙N+1S=\mathds{1}_{N+1}, we diagonalize H~\tilde{H}:

H~=W​D​W†,\tilde{H}=WDW^{\dagger}, (36)

where WW is the unitary matrix of eigenvectors and DD is the diagonal matrix of eigenvalues.

For separate-unitary cases where S≠𝟙N+1S\neq\mathds{1}_{N+1}, we solve the generalized eigenvalue problem:

H~​v=λ​S​v,\tilde{H}v=\lambda Sv, (37)

which can be transformed to standard form and yields eigenvectors that form the columns of matrix WW. The lowest (most negative) eigenvalue identifies the true ground state.

This transformation redefines our basis to the true orthonormal eigenstates. The true ground state is:

|χtrue[0]⟩=W00​|χ[0]⟩+∑i=1NW0​i​|χi[1]⟩,|\chi^{[0]}_{\mathrm{true}}\rangle=W_{00}|\chi^{[0]}\rangle+\sum_{i=1}^{N}W_{0i}|\chi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle, (38)

and the true 1QP eigenstates are

|χi,true[1]⟩=Wi​0​|χ[0]⟩+∑j=1NWi​j​|χj[1]⟩for ​i=1,…,N.|\chi^{[1]}_{i,\mathrm{true}}\rangle=W_{i0}|\chi^{[0]}\rangle+\sum_{j=1}^{N}W_{ij}|\chi^{[1]}_{j}\rangle\quad\text{for }i=1,\ldots,N. (39)

The matrices in this new basis are

𝒪true\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{true}} =\displaystyle= W†​𝒪,\displaystyle W^{\dagger}\mathcal{O}, (40)
H~true\displaystyle\quad\tilde{H}_{\mathrm{true}} =\displaystyle= W†​H~​W=D,\displaystyle W^{\dagger}\tilde{H}W=D,
Strue\displaystyle\quad S_{\mathrm{true}} =\displaystyle= W†​S​W=𝟙N+1,\displaystyle W^{\dagger}SW=\mathds{1}_{N+1},

where Strue=𝟙N+1S_{\mathrm{true}}=\mathds{1}_{N+1} confirms that the transformed states are orthonormal. For the generalized eigenvalue problem with non-orthogonal initial states (S≠𝟙N+1S\neq\mathds{1}_{N+1}), the matrix WW obtained from the eigenvalue solver is not unitary. The transformation can be equivalently understood as a two-step process: First preorthogonalize the basis using the symmetric orthogonalization (S†S)−1/2(S^{\dagger}S)^{-1/2}, and then apply a unitary transformation to diagonalize the Hamiltonian in the orthogonal basis. The generalized eigenvalue solver performs both steps simultaneously, directly producing orthonormal eigenvectors with respect to the metric SS.

For single-unitary variance cost functions (CvarGS,1​Q​PC_{\mathrm{var}}^{\mathrm{GS,1QP}}) with successful optimization, S=𝟙N+1S=\mathds{1}_{N+1} already, but diagonalizing H~\tilde{H} can still improve state quality by finding exact eigenstates within the VQE-prepared subspace.

We proceed to Step 2 using the transformed matrices. For notational simplicity, we drop the true subscript and continue to denote the VQE-prepared states as |χ[0]⟩|\chi^{[0]}\rangle and |χi[1]⟩|\chi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle, understanding these now refer to the orthonormalized eigenstates. The matrices 𝒪\mathcal{O}, H~\tilde{H}, and SS refer to these corrected, orthonormalized versions.

Step 2: Construct modified overlap matrix using PCAT recursion.

According to the PCAT prescription (Sec. III.3), modified states eliminate projections onto lower-energy subspaces of H0H_{0}. For the 1QP sector, the recursion from Eq. (17) is

|χ~i[1]⟩=|χi[1]⟩−⟨Φ[0]|χi[1]⟩⟨Φ[0]|χ[0]⟩​|χ[0]⟩|\widetilde{\chi}^{[1]}_{i}\rangle=|\chi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle-\frac{\langle\Phi^{[0]}|\chi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle}{\langle\Phi^{[0]}|\chi^{[0]}\rangle}|\chi^{[0]}\rangle (41)

for i=1,…,Ni=1,\ldots,N. Taking the overlap with an unperturbed state |Φj⟩|\Phi^{j}\rangle yields

⟨Φj[0]|χ~i[1]⟩\displaystyle\langle\Phi^{[0]}_{j}|\widetilde{\chi}^{[1]}_{i}\rangle =\displaystyle= ⟨Φj[0]|χi[1]⟩−⟨Φ[0]|χi[1]⟩⟨Φ[0]|χ[0]⟩​⟨Φj[0]|χ[0]⟩\displaystyle\langle\Phi^{[0]}_{j}|\chi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle-\frac{\langle\Phi^{[0]}|\chi^{[1]}_{i}\rangle}{\langle\Phi^{[0]}|\chi^{[0]}\rangle}\langle\Phi^{[0]}_{j}|\chi^{[0]}\rangle (42)
=\displaystyle= 𝒪i​j−𝒪i​0𝒪00​𝒪0​j.\displaystyle\mathcal{O}_{ij}-\frac{\mathcal{O}_{i0}}{\mathcal{O}_{00}}\mathcal{O}_{0j}.

The modified overlap matrix 𝒪~\widetilde{\mathcal{O}} for the 1QP sector is an N×(N+1)N\times(N+1) matrix:

𝒪~i​j=𝒪i​j−𝒪i​0𝒪00​𝒪0​j\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}_{ij}=\mathcal{O}_{ij}-\frac{\mathcal{O}_{i0}}{\mathcal{O}_{00}}\mathcal{O}_{0j} (43)

for rows i=1,…,Ni=1,\ldots,N (1QP states) and columns j=0,1,…,Nj=0,1,\ldots,N (all unperturbed states). Restricting to the 1QP subspace of H0H_{0} (columns j=1,…,Nj=1,\ldots,N), we obtain the N×NN\times N modified overlap matrix:

X~i​k[1]=𝒪i,k−𝒪i​0𝒪00​𝒪0,k\widetilde{X}^{[1]}_{ik}=\mathcal{O}_{i,k}-\frac{\mathcal{O}_{i0}}{\mathcal{O}_{00}}\mathcal{O}_{0,k} (44)

for i,k=1,…,Ni,k=1,\ldots,N. This ensures that P[0]​|χ~i[1]⟩=0P^{[0]}|\widetilde{\chi}^{[1]}_{i}\rangle=0 for all 1QP states.

Step 3: Construct the PCAT correction unitary.

The PCAT correction within the 1QP subspace is the N×NN\times N unitary matrix:

V[1]=X~[1]†(X~[1]X~[1]†)−1/2.V^{[1]}=\widetilde{X}^{[1]\dagger}(\widetilde{X}^{[1]}\widetilde{X}^{[1]\dagger})^{-1/2}. (45)

This corresponds to the transformation described in Sec. III.3, where the full PCAT unitary for the 1QP block is UPCAT[1]=U[1]​V[1]U_{\mathrm{PCAT}}^{[1]}=U^{[1]}V^{[1]}, with U[1]U^{[1]} being the matrix whose columns are the VQE-approximated 1QP eigenstates. Here, V[1]V^{[1]} represents the additional correction needed beyond the VQE unitary to enforce cluster additivity.

Step 4: Extract the effective 1QP Hamiltonian

The effective 1QP Hamiltonian is obtained by restricting the Hamiltonian matrix (from Step 1) to the 1QP sector and applying the PCAT correction. We extract the N×NN\times N subblock corresponding to the 1QP sector (rows and columns with indices 1,…,N1,\ldots,N) from the (N+1)×(N+1)(N+1)\times(N+1) transformed Hamiltonian. This restriction removes the ground state (index 0) and isolates the 1QP subspace:

H~i​j[1]=H~i,jfor ​i,j∈{1,…,N}.\tilde{H}^{[1]}_{ij}=\tilde{H}_{i,j}\quad\text{for }i,j\in\{1,\ldots,N\}. (46)

The effective 1QP Hamiltonian is then

Heff[1]=V[1]†H~[1]V[1]−E[0].H_{\mathrm{eff}}^{[1]}=V^{[1]\dagger}\tilde{H}^{[1]}V^{[1]}-E^{[0]}. (47)

This polynomial-time classical computation transforms the VQE output, encapsulated in the three matrices 𝒪\mathcal{O}, SS, and H~\tilde{H}, into the cluster-additive effective Hamiltonian required for NLCE. The resulting Heff[1]H_{\mathrm{eff}}^{[1]} is an N×NN\times N matrix in the 1QP basis, which after subtracting the ground-state energy E[0]E^{[0]}, gives the effective 1QP Hamiltonian for the cluster as defined in Sec. III:

Heff,C[1]=(UPCAT,C†​H​UPCAT,C)[11]−EC[0]H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},C}=(U_{\mathrm{PCAT},C}^{\dagger}HU_{\mathrm{PCAT},C})^{[11]}-E^{[0]}_{C} (48)

This quantity is then used in the NLCE embedding procedure [Eq. (7)] to obtain the 1QP dispersion in the thermodynamic limit.

V Applications

We now apply the NLCE+VQE approach of the previous sections to compute 1QP excitation energies in the TFIM. We investigate the one-dimensional chain at the critical point, the two-dimensional square lattice at its quantum critical point, and additionally the one-dimensional TFIM with longitudinal field (TFIM+LF) in the disordered phase. The longitudinal field fundamentally changes the model by breaking parity symmetry, coupling ground state to excitations, and making the one-dimensional model nonintegrable.

To benchmark NLCE+VQE, we compare its performance with NLCE++ED, where ED is used to compute properties on finite clusters. Furthermore, we investigate whether the variance- and trace-based cost functions yield similar results or not. In all three cases, we use the conjugate gradient method for the classical optimization in the VQE process.

V.1 Transverse-field Ising model

The 1D TFIM is one of the paradigmatic models for studying quantum phase transitions driven by quantum fluctuations. The Hamiltonian of the TFIM is given by

H=−h∑νZν−J∑<ν′,ν>Xν′Xν,H=-h\sum_{\nu}Z_{\nu}-J\sum_{<\nu^{\prime},\nu>}X_{\nu^{\prime}}X_{\nu^{\phantom{\prime}}}, (49)

where ZνZ_{\nu} and XνX_{\nu} denote the Pauli matrices acting on site ν\nu, JJ represents the nearest-neighbor Ising exchange coupling, and hh the strength of the transverse field. Throughout this work, we set h=1h=1 as our energy unit, such that all energies are measured in units of the transverse-field strength, and we consider ferromagnetic J>0J>0. For h=0h=0, the ground state is doubly degenerate, corresponding to ferromagnetic order along the xx axis and spontaneous breaking of the global ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry generated by ∏νXν\prod_{\nu}X_{\nu}. In contrast, for J=0J=0, the ground state is a product state of spins polarized along the zz direction, forming a paramagnetic phase that preserves ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry. The competition between these two noncommuting terms leads to a quantum critical point at JcJ_{c} separating the ordered and disordered phases.

The TFIM in one dimension is exactly solvable via Jordan-Wigner transformation [49], making it an ideal starting benchmark for validating our NLCE+VQE framework. In higher dimensions, the TFIM becomes nonintegrable but retains the same qualitative features. We perform expansions from the high-field polarized phase where the ground state is gapped and 1QP excitations correspond to localized spin flips, and study the quantum critical point where the gap closes.

V.1.1 One-dimensional chain

The one-dimensional TFIM undergoes a second-order phase transition at Jc=1J_{c}=1. The system is disordered when J<1J<1 and ordered (Ising ferromagnetic) when J>1J>1. We perform an expansion from the disordered phase as the unperturbed limit and present NLCE+VQE results at the critical point.

The exact 1QP dispersion in the thermodynamic limit is given by

ωexact​(k)=2​1+J2−2​J​cos⁡(k),\omega_{\mathrm{exact}}(k)=2\sqrt{1+J^{2}-2J\cos{(k)}}, (50)

where kk labels the momentum quantum number of the 1QP state, k∈[−π,π]k\in[-\pi,\pi]. At the critical point Jc=1J_{c}=1, the excitation gap closes at k=0k=0, resulting in a linear dispersion ω⁡(k)∝|k|\omega(k)\propto|k| characteristic of the (1+1)(1+1)-dimensional Ising universality class. This vanishing gap at criticality provides a stringent test of NLCE convergence.

For the one-dimensional chain, rectangular graphs have dimensions Lm×1≤NmaxL_{m}\times 1\leq N_{\mathrm{max}}. The embedding factors in NLCE are equal to 11. Hence, the expansion reduces to the contributions from only two clusters corresponding to NN and N−1N-1 and the terms corresponding to smaller clusters cancel out. The dispersion ω⁡(k)\omega(k) in the momentum states kk for one-dimensional chain can thus be written as

ω⁡(k)\displaystyle\omega(k) =\displaystyle= ∑ν,μNHeff,N,ν,μ[1]​ei​k​(ν−μ)\displaystyle\sum_{\nu,\mu}^{N}H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},N,\nu,\mu}\,e^{{\rm i}\,k\,(\nu-\mu)} (51)
−\displaystyle- ∑ν′,μ′N−1Heff,N−1,ν′​μ′[1]​ei​k​(ν′−μ′),\displaystyle\sum_{\nu^{\prime},\mu^{\prime}}^{N-1}H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},N-1,\nu^{\prime}\mu^{\prime}}\,e^{{\rm i}\,k\,(\nu^{\prime}-\mu^{\prime})},

where Heff,N,ν​μ[1]H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},N,\nu\mu} are the matrix elements of HeffH_{\mathrm{eff}} obtained with VQE for a hopping from site ν\nu to site μ\mu for a cluster NN given by ⟨ν|Heff,N[1]|μ⟩\langle\nu|H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},N}|\mu\rangle. The matrix Heff,N[1]H^{[1]}_{\mathrm{eff},N} for a cluster of size NN is given in Eq. 48.

Remarkably, for the one-dimensional TFIM, the VQE unitary optimized solely to minimize ground-state energy automatically decouples all excitation sectors simultaneously. This is a special property of this model that warrants explanation. After the Jordan-Wigner transformation, the 1D TFIM maps to a free-fermion model described by a quadratic Hamiltonian. In such systems, a single Bogoliubov transformation diagonalizes the entire Hamiltonian across all quasiparticle sectors. The VQE unitary UVQEU_{\mathrm{VQE}} effectively learns this Bogoliubov transformation when minimizing the ground-state energy. Importantly, while any block-diagonalization method must decouple the ground state from excitations, for a generic non-integrable system it would generally not decouple all higher quasiparticle sectors from each other.
